title: Soft Pull vs. Hard Pull: What Is the Difference and Why Does It Matter
summary: A soft credit pull checks your credit without affecting your score, while a hard credit pull happens when you apply for new credit and can temporarily lower your score by a few points. The difference matters because hard inquiries are visible to other lenders and can influence future credit decisions, whereas soft inquiries remain invisible to everyone but you.
body_markdown:
This guide covers how each inquiry type works, when they occur, how long they stay on your report, and how to minimize hard pull impact when shopping for financing.


‍


### What is a soft credit pull


A soft credit pull is a basic review of your credit file that happens without a formal credit application. The key thing to know: soft pulls do not affect your credit score. They may or may not show up on your credit report depending on the bureau, but even when they do appear, only you can see them.


Soft pulls happen more often than most people realize. When you check your own credit score through a free monitoring app, that's a soft pull. When a credit card company sends you a "pre-approved" offer in the mail, they ran a soft pull to see if you might qualify. Employers running background checks, insurance companies quoting rates, and your existing creditors reviewing your account all trigger soft pulls too.


- **Definition:** A preliminary credit file review not connected to a formal application
- **Credit score impact:** None
- **Visibility:** Only you can see soft inquiries on your report


The practical takeaway here is that you can check your own credit as often as you want without any downside. Soft pulls are essentially invisible to the lending world.


‍


### What is a hard credit pull


A hard credit pull is a formal request by a lender to review your credit report, and it only happens when you apply for new credit. Unlike soft pulls, hard pulls require your permission. They also show up on your credit report where other lenders can see them, and they can temporarily lower your score by a few points.


Hard pulls signal to lenders that you're actively seeking new debt. One hard inquiry on its own is usually not a big deal. But several hard inquiries clustered together can make lenders cautious, since it might suggest you're taking on more credit than you can handle.


- **Definition:** A formal lender request triggered when you apply for new credit
- **Credit score impact:** Can temporarily lower your score by a few points
- **Visibility:** Other lenders can see hard inquiries on your report


Common situations that trigger hard pulls include applying for a credit card, mortgage, auto loan, personal loan, or new line of credit.


‍


### Key differences between soft pulls and hard pulls


The core distinction comes down to three things: whether you gave permission, who can see the inquiry, and whether it affects your score.


Soft pulls often happen without your explicit approval. A credit card company can check your file to send you a pre-qualified offer without asking first. Hard pulls, on the other hand, always require your consent because they're tied to an actual credit application you submitted.


Factor Soft Pull Hard Pull


Your permission required Often no Yes


Affects credit score No Yes


Visible to lenders No Yes


Appears on your report Sometimes Yes


From a lender's perspective, soft inquiries don't exist. When a bank reviews your credit file to decide whether to approve your loan, they only see hard inquiries. Soft pulls remain completely hidden from anyone[evaluating your creditworthiness](https://www.lendflow.com/post/beyond-credit-scores-lendflow-redefines-kyc) .


‍


### How soft and hard credit inquiries affect your credit score


Soft inquiries have zero effect on your credit score. Credit scoring models exclude them entirely. You could check your own score every single day, and it wouldn't change a thing.


Hard inquiries work differently. Each one can reduce your score temporarily, though the drop is usually modestHard inquiries work differently. Each one can reduce your score temporarily, though the drop is usually modest —


[only 14% lose more than 10 points](https://www.hillsbank.com/how-much-do-credit-inquiries-affect-your-credit-score) from inquiries


. The impact tends to fade within a few months, and after 12 months, most scoring models stop factoring hard inquiries into your score calculation at all.


Here's where it gets a bit more nuanced.[Credit scoring models](https://www.lendflow.com/post/build-credit-scoring-model-lendflow) recognize that comparison shopping is normal behavior. If you're[shopping for a mortgage and apply with three different lenders](https://www.lendflow.com/post/marketplace-lending-vs-traditional-bank-loans-what-lenders-should-know) in the same week, those three inquiries typically count as just one inquiry for scoring purposes. The window varies by scoring model, ranging from 14 to 45 days, but the principle is the same: rate shopping for a single loan type won't tank your score.


What does raise red flags is applying for multiple different types of credit in a short period. Applying for a credit card, a personal loan, and an auto loan all in the same month looks very different from shopping around for the best mortgage rate.


‍


### Examples of soft and hard credit inquiries


Knowing which activities trigger each type of inquiry helps you anticipate what will and won't affect your credit.


#### Common soft credit pull examples


- Checking your own credit score through a monitoring service
- Receiving pre-qualified or pre-approved offers in the mail
- Employer background checks during hiring
- Insurance companies checking your credit for rate quotes
- Your existing creditors reviewing your account


#### Common hard credit pull examples


- Applying for a new credit card
- Applying for a mortgage
- Applying for an auto loan
- Applying for a personal loan
- Opening a new line of credit or retail store card


One thing worth noting: some services that advertise "pre-approval" actually run hard pulls. The terminology isn't always consistent across lenders. When in doubt, ask before you apply.


‍


### How long credit inquiries stay on your credit report


Hard inquiries remain on your credit report for about two years. However, their impact on your score typically fades much sooner, usually within the first 12 months. After two years, they drop off automatically without any action on your part.


Soft inquiries may appear on the version of your credit report that you see, but they stay hidden from creditors. Since soft pulls don't affect your score, there's no expiration date to worry about.


‍


### How many hard inquiries is too many


There's no universal cutoff that automatically disqualifies you from getting credit. That said, six or more hard inquiriesThere's no universal cutoff that automatically disqualifies you from getting credit. That said,


[six or more hard inquiries](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/credit-reports/credit-checks-and-inquiries) within a 12-month period can make some lenders hesitant, particularly for unsecured credit products like credit cards.


Context matters quite a bit here. A cluster of inquiries for the same loan type, like when you're comparing mortgage rates, looks very different from scattered applications for unrelated credit products. Lenders and scoring models both recognize the difference between responsible rate shopping and potential overextension.


The other factor is your overall credit profile. If you have a long credit history, low utilization, and no missed payments, a few hard inquiries probably won't move the needle much. If your credit file is thin or already shows some stress, each additional inquiry carries more weight.


‍


### How to minimize the impact of hard credit inquiries


A few practical approaches can help you manage hard inquiries without avoiding credit applications altogether.


#### Space out new credit applications


Rather than applying for several new accounts within a short window, spreading applications over time gives your score room to recover between inquiries. It also avoids the appearance of sudden credit-seeking behavior.


#### Use rate shopping windows when comparing offers


When comparing rates for a mortgage, auto loan, or student loan, doing your shopping within a concentrated timeframe works in your favor. Most scoring models treat multiple inquiries for the same loan type within a 14 to 45-day window as a single inquiry.


[within a 14 to 45-day window](https://www.ficoscore.com/faqs-about-fico-scores-us) as a single inquiry.


#### Prequalify with soft pulls before applying


Many lenders now offer prequalification that uses only a soft pull—often powered by a[credit data API](https://www.lendflow.com/post/credit-data-api-guide) . This lets you see estimated rates and terms before committing to a hard inquiry application. Modern[embedded lending platforms](https://www.lendflow.com/post/a-guide-to-embedded-lending) often enable soft-pull prequalification across multiple lenders through a single integration, so borrowers can compare offers without accumulating hard inquiries. Lendflow's platform, for example, supports soft-pull prequalification across 75+ lenders, helping brands offer financing experiences where borrowers can explore options without credit score impact.


‍


### How to dispute or remove a hard inquiry


If you spot a hard inquiry you didn't authorize, you can dispute it with the credit bureau. Unauthorized inquiries sometimes indicate identity theft or fraud, so investigating unfamiliar entries is worthwhile.


The basic dispute process looks like this:


- Obtain your credit report from each bureau (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion)
- Identify the unauthorized inquiry and note the creditor's name
- File a dispute directly with the credit bureau online, by mail, or by phone
- Provide supporting documentation if the bureau requests it


One important caveat: legitimate inquiries you authorized typically cannot be removed early. Even if you regret applying for that store credit card, the inquiry stays on your report until it falls off naturally after two years.


‍

### Frequently asked questions about soft and hard credit pulls


#### Can lenders see soft inquiries on my credit report?


No. Soft inquiries are only visible to you and do not appear on the version of your credit report that lenders review when making credit decisions.


#### Does prequalification always use a soft pull?


Most prequalification offers use soft pulls, but not all. Some lenders run hard pulls even for prequalification, so confirming with the lender before proceeding is a good idea.


#### Do soft pulls appear on business credit reports?


Business credit reporting works differently than personal credit. The soft versus hard inquiry distinction may vary by bureau and report type, so checking with the specific business credit bureau provides the most accurate answer.


#### Is a soft credit pull the same as a background check?


Not exactly. A background check may include a soft credit pull as one component, but background checks can also include criminal history, employment verification, and other non-credit information.
